meaning: Lord of the Earth (from πόσις + δᾶ)

phonemes.desc: Pi plus short omicron — the name plunges in with the sound of water striking.
Diphthong ει with no stress; the liquid middle syllable that carries the name across the wave.
Delta plus long omega with acute pitch — the stressed peak that holds like a swell before it breaks.

pronunciation.approximation: 'poh-SAY-done' — the second syllable is light, the third is long, pitched, and powerful.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: πόσις (posis), 'husband, lord' — a common Homeric epithet linked to his name

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *pótis, 'master, husband' — root of Greek πόσις and Latin potis

pronunciation.note: Poseidôn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ποσειδῶν contains both stress (circumflex on the long ω, realized as acute in our restoration) and length (ει diphthong and long ω). The circumflex form Poseidôn is the ideal; Poseidōn is the macron-only LSJ convention.

domains.title: The Earth-Shaker
domains.subtitle: Sea, Earthquakes, Horses, and Storms
domains.lead: Poseidôn is the lord of the waters that surround and threaten every Greek city. He is not a gentle sea; he is the earth-shaker, the tamer of horses, the sudden storm that overturns ships and cracks land. His power is older than Zeús in some traditions, and his rivalry with Athena for Athens defines the tension between maritime force and civic wisdom.

cards.name: The Open Sea
cards.desc: Poseidôn commands the Mediterranean itself — calm or wrathful, generous or deadly.

cards.name: Earthquake
cards.desc: His trident strikes rock and splits the earth; every tremor is his chariot passing beneath.

cards.name: Horses
cards.desc: He created the horse, either as a gift to Athens or as a creature of the breaking wave.

cards.name: Storms and Winds
cards.desc: The sudden gale, the waterspout, and the drowning wave all answer to him.

symbols.name: Trident
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over sea and earthquake; weapon and scepter combined

symbols.name: Horse
symbols.meaning: His gift to humanity and the breaker of waves made flesh

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial animal; the bull from the sea in myths of Minos

symbols.name: Dolphin
symbols.meaning: Messenger and rescuer; guides sailors and heroes

symbols.name: Pine tree
symbols.meaning: Sacred to him; wood for ship masts

symbols.name: Breaking wave
symbols.meaning: The sudden, irresistible force of his domain

mythology.lead: Poseidôn's myths dramatize the rage of the excluded. He is a great Olympian, yet he is repeatedly thwarted — by Athena at Athens, by Odysseus after the blinding of Polyphemus, by the very mortals whose sacrifices he demands.

myths.title: Lord of the Sea
myths.text: After the defeat of the Titans, Zeús, Poseidôn, and Hádês divided the cosmos by lot. Zeús took the sky, Hádês the underworld, and Poseidôn the sea. The earth remained common to all three. This tripartition makes Poseidôn equal in dignity to his brothers, yet his watery realm is restless and uncontainable — a fitting symbol of his temperament.

myths.title: Defeated by Athena
myths.text: Poseidôn and Athénā competed for the patronage of Athens. He struck the Acropolis with his trident and produced a salt spring; she planted the olive tree. The city chose her gift. Poseidôn flooded Attica in revenge, and the Athenians placated him by giving the first fruits of the harvest and by honoring Erechtheus, whom he had destroyed. The myth encodes the Greek insight that sea power must yield to civic wisdom.

myths.title: Odysseus and Polyphemus
myths.text: When Odysseus blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus — Poseidôn's son — the god pursued the hero across the sea for ten years. Every storm, every shipwreck, every near-drowning was Poseidôn's vengeance. Yet the god's wrath is also a narrative force: without it, the Odyssey would not exist. Poseidôn is the obstacle that makes the return meaningful.

myths.title: The Horse and the Foundation
myths.text: Poseidôn invented the horse, either in his failed bid for Athens or as a gift to mortals. The horse embodies his nature: beautiful, powerful, and potentially destructive. In Thessaly and Athens he was worshipped as Hippios, 'Horseman,' and chariot races honored him. The breaking wave and the galloping horse share the same curve and the same danger.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Poseidôn with Neptunus, an Italic water god associated with fresh water before Greek influence made him the sea. In later antiquity Poseidon-Neptune became one of the most recognizable gods of the Roman pantheon, his chariot drawn by hippocamps. In art he carries the trident that is still his universal attribute. The planet Neptune, discovered in 1846, bears his name. Modern culture uses him as the archetype of the stormy, vengeful sea god, from Renaissance frescoes to blockbuster films.
lore.culturalLegacy: Poseidôn's legacy is the recognition that the sea is never truly conquered. Every Greek colony, every fisherman, every sailor lived under his power. The Isthmian Games at Corinth honored him; sailors prayed to him before departure. His trident remains a symbol of maritime sovereignty, appearing on coins, naval insignia, and the flag of Barbados. In an age of climate change and rising seas, Poseidôn's ancient title 'Earth-Shaker' has taken on new literal force. Restoring Poseidôn restores the name by which the Greeks named the water that surrounds civilization.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Poseidôn is the god of what the Greeks could not control. The sea was not a highway to them; it was a vast, unpredictable power that could swallow cities. Earthquakes were even worse — no warning, no defense, no explanation except the anger of the god. Poseidôn therefore represents the limits of human mastery, the forces that mock our plans.

Yet he is also the giver of horses, one of the most useful and beautiful creatures in the ancient world. This double nature is typical of Greek religion: the same god who destroys also provides. To honor Poseidôn is not to deny danger but to acknowledge it, to build one's city with the sea in mind, to pray before sailing, and to accept that the earth may shake.
lore.archaeology: Sounion: Temple of Poseidon (ca. 444 BCE) on the Attic promontory. Isthmia: sanctuary and games of Poseidon from 582 BCE.
